title: Onsen Tamago
subtitle: slow-cooked soft egg in warm dashi broth
excerpt: Onsen tamago is a Japanese slow-cooked egg with a custard-soft white and a just-set, silky yolk, traditionally cooked in hot spring water. Served in a small bowl of warm dashi broth, it is a quietly perfect dish. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Onsen tamago, meaning 'hot spring egg', originates from Japan's hot spring resorts where eggs were cooked directly in the geothermal waters at around 65 to 70 degrees Celsius.

recipe.batchNotes: Up to 12 eggs can be cooked at once in the same pot. Serve within 30 minutes of cooking.
recipe.temperatureNote: Water temperature for cooking the eggs. Use an instant-read thermometer to maintain 68°C throughout the cooking time.

glossaryTerms.definition: An egg cooked at a precisely controlled low temperature of around 65 to 70°C, resulting in a custard-soft white and a thick, creamy, just-set yolk.
A light, seasoned dashi broth used to serve onsen tamago, made from dashi, soy sauce, and mirin.

content.text: is the result of cooking at a temperature where the yolk sets before the white does. The egg is lowered into water held at exactly 68°C and left for 13 minutes. Serve in a bowl of warm
Temperature control is the only skill this recipe requires. If your hob cannot hold 68°C, fill the pot with 68°C water, remove from heat, insulate with a towel, and leave for 20 minutes.
Fill a medium saucepan with enough water to submerge the eggs. Heat to exactly 68°C using an instant-read thermometer.
Lower the eggs gently into the water using a spoon. Maintain the temperature at 68°C for 13 minutes, adjusting the heat up or down as needed.
While the eggs cook, combine dashi, soy sauce, and mirin in a small saucepan. Warm gently over low heat until just steaming. Do not boil.
Remove the eggs from the water with a spoon. Crack each egg carefully into a small bowl by tapping the shell gently. The white should be barely set and soft around the yolk.
Pour 50 ml of warm tsuyu broth into each bowl around the egg. Top with spring onion, nori, and bonito flakes. Serve immediately.

attrs.symptom: Yolk is still liquid and runny
attrs.cause: The water temperature dropped too low during cooking.
attrs.fix: Check the thermometer every 3 minutes and adjust the heat. Add a small splash of hot water if temperature drops.

attrs.symptom: White is rubbery and fully set
attrs.cause: The water was too hot, above 70°C.
attrs.fix: Add cold water to the pot immediately to drop the temperature, then check the eggs after another 5 minutes.

attrs.symptom: Egg breaks apart when cracked into the bowl
attrs.cause: The shell was cracked too aggressively or the egg was shaken.
attrs.fix: Tap the widest part of the shell firmly with a teaspoon and peel away a small circle to let the egg slide out gently.

content.text: Onsen tamago comes from Japan's hot spring culture. Ryokan inns would lower baskets of eggs into the natural springs to cook overnight for breakfast. The specific temperature of hot spring water creates the unique texture by accident of geology. Home cooks replicate it with a thermometer and patience. It is one of the quietest, most elegant dishes in Japanese cooking.
